title: Next.js Patterns That Actually Scale
description: Practical patterns for building Next.js applications that remain maintainable as they grow from prototype to production.
content:
Most Next.js tutorials show you how to build a todo app. Here's what you need to know when your todo app becomes a platform serving millions of requests.

## Pattern 1: Route Handlers Over API Routes

With the App Router, route handlers are your friend. But structure them properly:

```typescript
// app/api/articles/route.ts
export async function GET(request: Request) {
  const { searchParams } = new URL(request.url);
  
  // Validate input early
  const page = parseInt(searchParams.get('page') || '1');
  const limit = Math.min(parseInt(searchParams.get('limit') || '10'), 50);
  
  // Business logic in a separate module, not in the route handler
  const articles = await articleService.list({ page, limit });
  
  return Response.json(articles);
}
```

## Pattern 2: Server Components as the Default

Use server components unless you specifically need interactivity. This isn't just a performance optimization — it changes how you think about data flow.

Server components can:
- Access databases directly
- Read files
- Use secrets safely
- Reduce client bundle size

Client components should be the exception, not the rule.

## Pattern 3: Colocation

Keep related files together. Don't create separate `components/`, `utils/`, `types/` directories at the root. Instead:

```
app/
  articles/
    page.tsx          # Server component
    ArticleList.tsx    # Client component (if needed)
    types.ts           # Article-specific types
    actions.ts         # Server actions
    utils.ts           # Article-specific utilities
```

This pattern scales much better than flat directory structures.

## Pattern 4: Error Boundaries at Every Level

Don't let one broken component crash your entire page. Wrap sections in error boundaries:

```tsx
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ArticleError />}>
  <ArticleContent />
</ErrorBoundary>
```

## Pattern 5: Streaming and Suspense

Use streaming to improve perceived performance:

```tsx
<Suspense fallback={<ArticleSkeleton />}>
  <ArticleContent slug={slug} />
</Suspense>
```

The user sees the layout immediately while content loads. This is the single biggest UX improvement you can make.

## The Meta-Pattern

The unifying theme: **move complexity to the server, keep the client simple**. Every time you're tempted to add a client-side state management library, ask yourself if this could be a server component instead.

Next.js is at its best when you let it do what it was designed to do.
